passages.title: Email Correspondence: A Home Care Schedule

emails.subject: Care visits for my father, client 3318 — timing
emails.body:
Dear Brightwater,

My father is 87 and has four home visits a day under his care package. I am writing about the timing, not the carers, who have been kind and competent without exception.

His contracted visits are breakfast, lunch, tea and bedtime. In practice the bedtime visit has arrived between 6:40 and 7:15 pm for the past six weeks. He is being put to bed before dark in July. He then wakes at two in the morning and sits in a chair until the breakfast visit at eight.

I understand the constraint. The bedtime round covers eleven clients and cannot serve them all at bedtime, and I am not asking you to send someone at nine simply because we would prefer it.

What I am asking is whether the order of the round is fixed. If my father is always last but one because that is how the route was built, and the route has never been revisited, then someone else is always first and my father is always at 6:45. If the order rotated weekly, everyone would get a reasonable bedtime some of the time. That may be impossible for reasons I cannot see, and I would accept that answer if it were the reason.

With thanks,
Rosalind Achebe

emails.subject: RE: Care visits for my father, client 3318 — timing
emails.body:
Dear Ms Achebe,

The order is not fixed and it has never been revisited. You have identified something nobody here had asked.

The evening route was built four years ago around geography — shortest driving distance between addresses — and has been inherited by every coordinator since, including me. Nobody chose the order your father sits in. It is simply the order that fell out of a mapping exercise, and it has quietly become a permanent allocation of the least desirable slot to the same four clients.

I have modelled a weekly rotation this morning. It adds about eleven minutes of driving to the round, which is absorbable. It starts on 21 July, and your father will be first on the round in week one, which puts his bedtime visit at approximately 8:45 pm.

Two things I should be straight about.

The rotation cannot include two clients who require a fixed evening time for medication reasons. They will remain in place, and that is clinical rather than convenience.

And the two-in-the-morning waking may not resolve with a later bedtime. It might, and I would not want you to expect it. If it persists, that is worth raising with his GP rather than with us, because it may be unrelated to the schedule entirely.

Regards,
Malika Benhaddou
Care Coordinator

passages.title: What Older People Actually Want From Where They Live
passages.content:
Policy on housing in later life is organised around a phrase — ageing in place — that almost everyone endorses and few examine. Surveys consistently find that older people wish to remain in their own homes, and that finding is used to justify a broad preference for home adaptation over any form of moving. The surveys are accurate. The inference drawn from them is frequently wrong.

What the more careful research finds is that the strong preference is for remaining in a familiar community rather than in a particular building. When the question separates the two, willingness to move within a known neighbourhood is substantially higher than willingness to leave it, and considerably higher than the headline figure suggests. A policy that funds stairlifts in unsuitable houses and builds nothing appropriate nearby is answering a question that was not asked.

The building itself matters in ways that are easy to measure and often ignored. Falls are the dominant cause of injury and lost independence in later life, and a large share occur on stairs, in bathrooms and at thresholds. Adaptations reduce that risk substantially, and yet uptake is limited by cost, by waiting lists for assessment, and by a factor rarely recorded: many people decline adaptations because they read them as an announcement that decline has begun. Presentation affects uptake as much as availability does.

Isolation is the outcome most strongly associated with poor health in this age group, and it correlates less with living alone than with the loss of routine reasons to leave the house. Someone living alone who shops daily and attends something weekly is in a different position from someone living with family who does neither. This distinction is invisible in the metrics usually collected, which count household composition rather than contact.

Transport is the constraint that determines whether any of the above is achievable. Where a bus route is withdrawn, the effect on an older population is not inconvenience but the removal of the mechanism by which shops, appointments and company are reached. Housing designed for later life in a location without transport reproduces the problem it was built to solve, at higher cost.

The practical conclusion is that the useful unit of planning is the neighbourhood rather than the dwelling: adapted homes are necessary and insufficient, and what determines whether later life goes well is largely what lies within a short walk of the front door.

passages.title: Should Care Costs Be Capped by Government?

viewpoints.name: Minister Cordelia Ashworth
viewpoints.text: We introduced a lifetime cap and I would defend it while accepting the criticism that it protects assets more than it protects people. That is true. The households that benefit most are those with something substantial to lose, and the poorest were already protected by means-testing. What the cap actually buys is the ability to plan — before it, no family could answer the question of what care might cost, because the honest answer was unbounded. I would rather argue for it on that basis than pretend it is redistributive.

viewpoints.name: Dr Ilya Sokolov, health economist
viewpoints.text: The cap is defensible and the arithmetic around it is routinely misrepresented, including by its supporters. It counts only personal care, not accommodation costs, so a family reaching the cap continues paying a substantial monthly sum indefinitely. Most people hear the word cap and understand it as a total. That gap between the policy and the public understanding of it is the real problem, and it will surface as anger at exactly the moment families are least able to absorb it.

viewpoints.name: Winifred Osei-Tutu, care home manager
viewpoints.text: My concern is the funding rate, not the cap. Local authority rates have not tracked wage costs, so homes cross-subsidise state-funded residents from self-funded ones, which means a self-funder pays more for the identical room and care. That is not a business model anyone designed; it is what happens when one rate is set below cost. A cap that increases the state-funded proportion without changing the rate accelerates a problem the sector already has, and homes will close before the policy is reviewed.

viewpoints.name: Tobias Lindgren, carer for his mother
viewpoints.text: I have given up work to care for my mother and I want to point out what the whole debate omits. Every projection of care costs assumes families like mine keep providing unpaid care, and none of them price it. My labour is the largest single input into her care and it appears in no budget. Cap the costs by all means, but if the model quietly depends on someone leaving employment to make the numbers work, say so, and then decide whether that is a policy or an accident.
